articleSummary: Satna, India — Two bacterial, contagious diseases threaten dairy cattle during the monsoon: Galghontu and Lame Fever. The critical window is late June to early July, with vaccination before the rains deemed essential. Galghontu causes sudden high fever, swelling of the throat, neck, or chest, excessive drooling, and labored breathing; Lame Fever causes swelling in thigh, shank, or shoulder muscles with lameness and a crepitus-like sound on palpation. Without prompt antibiotics, both diseases can prove fatal within 12–48 hours of symptoms. Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in DRC and Uganda prompted the WHO PHEIC on 17 May. By 8 June, 569 confirmed cases and 103 deaths; no approved specific treatment or vaccine. Transmission is via contact with blood or bodily fluids of symptomatic individuals. Imported European case was a doctor in France on 24 June.

articleSummary: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is in peak season in Guangdong, China, especially affecting children under 5 years old; preschool-age children are the main susceptible group, with infants under 6 months at higher risk of severe illness. The illness spreads mainly through contact with saliva, feces, and vesicle fluid, with infectiousness strongest within the first week after onset. Major symptoms include fever and painful oral ulcers in the early stage, leading to reduced appetite; later, a characteristic rash appears on hands and feet. Prevention centers on breaking transmission through hygiene and disinfection: isolate the child's items, disinfect with chlorine-based agents, and monitor for persistent high fever, lethargy, or seizures. Caregivers should wash hands before meals and after coming home, ventilate living spaces, and regularly disinfect utensils and toys; avoid crowded enclosed venues during peak season. EV71 vaccination is recommended for children 6 months–5 years, ideally two doses before 12 months of age with at least a 4-week interval; schools should implement routine checks and prompt reporting.

articleSummary: Canadian CMAJ series warns that Ebola and hantaviruses are increasingly masquerading as influenza. Early, non-specific symptoms—fever, myalgias, and headache—complicate initial diagnosis. Hantavirus infections in North America are typically linked to contact with infected rodents; Andes virus is notable for human-to-human transmission. There are no licensed antivirals or vaccines for hantavirus; management is supportive, reducing risk of severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome or kidney injury, with isolation to prevent spread, as airborne transmission is possible. Ebola's natural reservoir is fruit bats; transmission occurs via bodily fluids and contaminated surfaces. For Zaïre ebolavirus, antiviral therapies and a vaccine have reduced mortality to about 35%. The current Democratic Republic of Congo outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, with mortality up to 50% and no approved vaccines; rapid detection and strict hospital infection control are essential for survival.

articleHeadline: Never underestimate dengue | New Straits Times
articleSummary: Malaysia ranks third in ASEAN for dengue cases this year, with 33,367 cases reported as of June 13, a 20.7% rise from the same period last year. Indonesia has 39,672 and Vietnam 35,986. Dengue can deteriorate rapidly; warning signs include persistent high fever (39–40°C), abdominal pain, fatigue and vomiting, and severe dengue may follow the fever, causing plasma leakage, bleeding and organ failure. Leaking vessels can lead to fluid buildup in the lungs and abdomen, impairing breathing; platelets drop, raising bleeding risk. Dengue affects all ages; reinfection with a different strain can raise the risk of severe dengue, with four circulating strains. There is no specific cure; prevention is key: eliminate breeding grounds, remove standing water, use repellents, wear protective clothing, and install screens or nets. Seek early medical care; dengue can be detected on day one, and vaccination can be discussed with a doctor.

articleSummary: Orubosh virus, a dengue-like pathogen, may have infected about 9.4 million people across Latin America and the Caribbean since 1960, with Brazil accounting for roughly 5.5 million cases. A massive 2023 outbreak in Brazil, including the first confirmed death, raised international concern as transmission spread from the Amazon to urban centers. Manaus emerged as a major hotspot, with an estimated 300,000 infections in 2023–2024—about 260 times higher than officially reported. The illness causes fever, headache and myalgia and can lead to serious complications, including encephalitis and pregnancy loss. Manaus experienced two waves, in the 1980s and in 2023, each affecting more than 12% of residents. Studies in Nature Medicine and Nature Health, using mathematical modeling, historical data, and blood banks, suggest many infections remain undetected. Orubosh is transmitted by the Gunpowder Midge, a tiny vector thriving in rural forests, complicating urban spraying. Researchers call for rural-focused surveillance, genomic analysis, and integrated environmental-immunological-epidemiological data systems as early warning.

articleHeadline: What Is Typhus?
articleSummary: Typhus is an infection transmitted to humans by lice, fleas, and mites, treatable with antibiotics. Three types are described: endemic (murine) typhus in tropical/subtropical regions spread by fleas from rodents (bacteria: Rickettsia typhi); louse (epidemic) typhus globally, more common in Asia, Africa, and Mexico, with U.S. cases linked to flying squirrels (bacteria: Rickettsia prowazekii); and scrub (bush) typhus in rural northern Australia, Southeast Asia, India, Indonesia, Japan, and China, transmitted by chiggers (Orientia tsutsugamushi). Symptoms vary by type; scrub typhus includes headaches, fever, cough, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, chills, body/muscle aches, a bite-site scab, lymph node inflammation, and rash, with possible severe neurological involvement. Murine typhus is usually milder; mortality drops with timely antibiotics. Untreated typhus can cause long-term effects and rare Brill-Zinsser relapse. Diagnosis uses skin biopsy, immunofluorescence, serology, or PCR. Treatments include tetracycline, doxycycline, and azithromycin. Prevention emphasizes avoiding rodents and wild animals.

Built on 'one team, one plan, one budget,' it brings together experts in surveillance, laboratory systems, case management, infection prevention and control, emergency logistics and operations, risk communication, information management, and partner coordination. The move supports Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease efforts and regional collaboration under Africa CDC, WHO, and the African Union. Ebola is highly contagious with an average fatality rate around 50%, with past outbreaks ranging 25–90%; the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak began in Guinea and spread to Sierra Leone and Liberia.

articleSummary: Shenzhen, China reports multiple families infected with scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei), a highly contagious skin disease spread by close contact and contaminated furnishings. In one afternoon, Shenzhen Skin Disease Hospital treated 3 scabies-affected families, totaling about 7–8 patients, after a school dormitory case led to household transmission. Symptoms include intense nocturnal itching and red papules, with small linear skin tunnels on exposed areas such as fingers, wrists, armpits, abdomen, and inner thighs; head and face are less affected. Diagnosis relies on skin scraping or dermoscopy to visualize mites in superficial tunnels. Treatment requires topical antiparasitic medications plus environmental decontamination: high-temperature washing and sun-drying of bedding, disinfecting or replacing mattresses, and thorough cleaning of objects. Anti-allergic therapy alone is ineffective; all household members should be treated to prevent reinfection, and avoid sharing towels or personal items.

articleSummary: Japanese encephalitis (JEV) outbreaks and fatalities are reported across Vietnam as of June 29, 2026. articleSummary: Ebola virus outbreak in Africa centers on fruit bats as the natural reservoir, with transmission to other animals and humans via direct contact with infected animals or their secretions, particularly among hunters in forested areas. A medical expert states home pets pose no risk and are not infection sources. The virus is not spread by cooked meat, since cooking kills it; infection occurs through contact with animal secretions or via mucous membranes or skin. Most fatalities have occurred in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with cases reported in Uganda; the current outbreak has reached about 740 cases. Fatality rates can range from 30% to 50%, underscoring Ebola’s high virulence and global concern. Domestic pets are not implicated; exposure remains linked to direct contact with infected animals or their Secretions in rural or bush settings.

articleSummary: Japanese encephalitis is surging in Vietnam this summer, with nationwide hospitals reporting severe cases and fatalities. A 14-year-old girl from Dong Son Ward, Thanh Hoa Province, died after rapid progression from fever, headache, vomiting and fatigue to slurred speech, altered consciousness and increased muscle tone despite intensive care. Doctors from the Tropical Diseases Center at the National Pediatric Hospital warn early JE mimics influenza or gastroenteritis, delaying diagnosis; rapid deterioration can cause seizures, coma and multi-organ failure. There is no specific antiviral treatment; vaccination is the best preventive measure. The national immunization program provides three primary doses at age 1, then after 1–2 weeks and after one year, with boosters every 3–4 years until 15. Booster neglect leaves older children and adults at risk.
